source.title: Finding features in Transformers: Contrastive directions elicit stronger low-level perturbation responses than baselines

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether candidate SAE directions produce a distinctive downstream response and reports that they behave similarly to random directions, refining and challenging their status as computational features. It does not test the toy-model superposition mechanism itself.
record.gate_note: The study measures downstream responses to perturbations along contrastive, SAE and random directions in LLMs. Prior-work findings cited in the post are not rows. Figure values are not stated numerically in the text. The comment's separate steering result (~80% Mandarin tokens at ~20 degrees) is not a test of the claim versions about SAE units or representation geometry.
record.test_reason: The study perturbs LLM activations along SAE feature directions and reports that the model treats them like random directions, not like contrastive concept directions. This is direct, though preliminary, evidence against SAE features being the model's computational units (V5). It does not measure feature spread across neurons or how well a dictionary recovers sparse features (V4), nor any toy-model, polysemanticity or dimensionality question.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that contrastive directions elicit qualitatively stronger low-magnitude responses than SAE or random directions, and that SAE directions are not treated specially by the model, which is evidence against SAEs finding true computational features. They frame the perturbation test as a promising, preliminary way to identify features. They also note that plateaus may reflect error correction, but do not test this.
record.recipe_differences: This is an LLM activation-perturbation comparison of contrastive, SAE and random directions, not the toy-network construction and geometric analysis of the original superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The study varies concept pair, model, perturbation layer, constant-norm versus additive perturbation, and downstream response metric. Layer 2 produces stronger plateaus than layer 8; the contrastive-versus-other-directions difference is reported to persist.

fits_no_version.finding: Difference-of-means concept directions break through the activation-perturbation plateau at much smaller angles than random or SAE directions. This anisotropic sensitivity holds across models, layers, metrics and perturbation schemes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM activations show anisotropic perturbation sensitivity: some concept directions are privileged relative to random directions, consistent with suppression of interference from superposed features.

record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong research update; peer review not stated
record.problems: Preliminary research update. The reported curves are figures without numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text. Tests only selected models, layers, direction types and concept pairs; it does not directly assess feature completeness, stability, or the toy-model geometry.
record.rows_left_out: The post says SAE features selected randomly from the dictionary and features active on the opposite class gave similar results, but does not provide separately attributable model- and condition-specific outcomes. It also describes the results only qualitatively for these variants.

untested.parts: Completeness, stability across SAE runs or datasets, and canonicality are not tested. Only the functional distinctiveness of top-activating SAE features under perturbation is tested.
Untested: feature distribution across neurons, and whether SAEs recover sparse features (reconstruction, sparsity, interpretability).
Untested: the study assumes 1-D directions and makes no comparison with multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: This is a preliminary LessWrong research update. All results are figure-only, with no numbers or uncertainty given. The random-direction rows (r3, r6, etc.) are correctly control rows with versions 'none', and should serve as the baseline for the SAE rows. The SAE variants (random dictionary features, opposite-class features) are declared in rows_left_out. The steering result in the comments (~80% Mandarin tokens at ~20°) concerns contrastive directions and bears on no version. The study cites Elhage et al. 2022 only as background.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-count-to-dimension ratio, sparsity sweep, or regular geometry is tested.
No neuron polysemanticity, capacity competition, or feature-importance comparison is measured.
No polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity are examined.

Tests the downstream response to selected SAE directions, not whether features are spread across neurons, how many neurons represent them, or whether the dictionary recovers a complete set of sparse features.
Tests downstream perturbation response as a functional criterion; does not establish completeness, stability across settings, or canonical status of SAE features generally.
The study assumes candidate concepts are directions but does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features.

relationships.condition: Top-activating SAE features at early layers (2/7, plus layer 8) in Gemma 2-9B, Llama 3.1-8B and Qwen 3-1.7B, across three concept pairs, two perturbation schemes and three response metrics
relationships.reason: SAE directions need the same large perturbations as random directions to break the activation plateau, while contrastive directions respond early. The authors call this 'evidence against SAEs finding the true computational features'. Rows r2, r5, r8, r11, r14, r17, r20, r23, r26. This is figure-only and preliminary, and similarity to random holds 'in most cases'.
relationships.display_finding: Like random directions, SAE directions needed large perturbations to break the activation plateau, while contrastive directions responded early. The authors read this as evidence against SAEs finding the true computational features, but the result is preliminary and holds only in most cases.
